transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Um, hi Doctor. It's nice to meet you. I, uh... well, my lieutenant at the station actually sent me. It’s a little embarrassing, to be honest, and I really don't want to make a big deal out of it, but I want to be cooperative with you. 

I was just... I was organizing our equipment. The airway bags. I kept moving them into this specific pattern that I just knew was right, and I guess I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud while I did it. Just trying to be thorough, you know? But then my lieutenant told me to stop, and... I didn't step away. I didn't mean to be insubordinate or cause trouble, I swear, it's just... it felt like the whole ambulance bay would go bad if I broke the sequence right then. 

I hope I'm explaining that okay? I really am just trying to do the right thing, I promise. Does that make sense?

When you're doing that pattern with the equipment and repeating the numbers, do you feel like the urge is excessive or doesn't make sense, or does it feel like just the right and reasonable way to do the job?

Um... well, I guess when you put it like that, I can totally see how it might look a little excessive to someone else. I really don't want to be unreasonable, I promise. I know how it must have looked to my lieutenant. 

But in the moment, it just... it feels completely right. Like it's the only safe way to set up the bags. I just want to be thorough so nothing goes wrong on a call, you know? It feels like the most responsible thing to do at the time. I'm really trying to understand his side of it, though, because I want to be a good medic and I don't want to cause any problems for the station. 

I hope that's an okay answer? I'm really trying to explain it the right way for you.

When your lieutenant told you to stop and interrupted the sequence, what did you actually feel inside—was it intense anxiety or dread, like something bad might happen, or was it more just annoyance that he was getting in the way of doing things the 'right' way?

Um... well, it wasn't annoyance. I'd never want to be annoyed with my lieutenant, he's a really good guy and a great boss. I respect him a lot. 

But when he told me to stop, it... it was more like this awful, sinking dread. I just... I couldn't step away. I know I should have, and I feel terrible that I didn't listen to him right away, but it really felt like if I didn't finish moving the airway bags into that exact pattern, and if I didn't finish saying the dispatch numbers... like the whole ambulance bay would just go bad. Like something terrible would happen to the station if I broke the sequence right then. 

I know that probably sounds strange, and I'm really sorry if I'm not making sense. I just felt so much pressure to keep everyone safe by finishing it. Does that... does that answer your question okay? I want to make sure I'm giving you what you need.

Does this need to arrange things in a very particular way and repeat certain words or numbers happen in lots of different areas of your life—like at home, with your own belongings, or in other daily routines—or is it really just tied to specific situations like this equipment setup at work?

Um... well, it's... I guess it's mostly just at work? I mean, I really try to keep things normal at home. I don't want to be difficult to live with or anything. 

I guess... sometimes I might, you know, line up my boots in a certain way before a shift, or maybe I'll count the keys on my ring just to make sure they're all there. But it's not a big deal, I promise. It's just little things here and there to stay organized. I really don't think it's as intense as the airway bags at the station. I try really hard to just be easygoing when I'm off the clock. 

Is that... is that the kind of thing you were asking about? I hope I'm not making it sound worse than it is. I really am trying to keep it all under control.

Aside from the actual repeating and arranging behaviors, do you also get unwanted, intrusive thoughts or images that pop into your head—separate from the urge to do the ritual—that you find disturbing or hard to push away?

Um... no, not really. I mean, I definitely don't have anything disturbing or... or bad popping into my head. I'm a really positive person, I try to keep my mind focused on good things and just doing my job well. 

I guess sometimes I just think about the dispatch numbers, like I mentioned, but it's not... it's not like a scary thought or anything I can't handle. I just want to make sure I'm doing everything right. I don't have any, like, weird or upsetting images or anything like that. I promise I'm completely normal in that way. 

Does that make sense? I really hope I'm answering these the way you need me to. I just want to be helpful.

I'm... I'm really sorry, doctor, I don't think I quite caught what you just asked. My mind just drifted for a split second. 

Could you maybe repeat that for me? I really want to make sure I'm answering you properly and giving you exactly what you need to know. I'm trying my best to be a good patient and be helpful, I promise. I just didn't quite hear the question.
About how much time each day do you spend on these arranging and counting rituals, and would you say they cause you significant distress or get in the way of your daily responsibilities?

Um... well, as for the time, I really try not to let it take up too much of my day. I want to be productive, you know? But... I guess if I'm being completely honest, and I really want to be open with you... it has gotten a little bit in the way. It's actually a little embarrassing to admit. 

I'm... I'm not actually working on the ambulance anymore. They had me step back from the rig. They moved me to desk duty for a while, which was fine, I was really trying my best to be helpful there! But I guess my notes and the equipment checks started getting a little... unreliable. So they ended up taking me off the schedule completely. Just for right now, I'm sure. 

And I guess because of all that, I've mostly stopped seeing my friends lately, or... or keeping up with things at home the way I used to. I just haven't been as social, just trying to keep my head down and stay out of people's way. 

I hope it's okay that I shared that. I know it probably sounds like I'm not doing very well, but I really am trying hard to get everything back in order and be a good employee again. Did I answer that right for you? I just want to make sure I'm giving you what you need.

When you feel that urge to arrange things or repeat the numbers, do you ever try to resist or stop yourself from doing it, even briefly, before giving in—or does it not really feel like something you're fighting against, just something you need to do?

Um... resist it? I mean, I... I don't really fight it, no. It's not like a big struggle or anything bad like that. 

I just... I just do it. It feels like something I'm supposed to do, you know? Like it's just part of my routine, making sure everything is lined up right and the numbers are correct. It doesn't feel like a bad habit I need to break or anything. It's just... it's just what I do to make sure things are handled properly. 

I don't want you to think I'm out of control or anything, doctor. I'm really not. I just prefer things a certain way. Is that... does that make sense? I hope that's the kind of answer you were looking for. I'm really trying to explain it right for you.

Um... I'm not really sure about that one, doctor. I haven't really noticed anything like that happening with me. 

I... I hope it's okay that I don't have a better answer for you. I'm really trying my best to give you all the information you need, I promise. I just don't think I've experienced that. Does that make sense? I can try to think a little harder about it if you need me to, I just want to make sure I'm being a good patient for you.

Has this strong need for things to be arranged 'just right' and done in a very particular order been part of who you are since you were young—like a lifelong personality trait—or is this something that started or got noticeably worse more recently?

Um... well, no, it definitely hasn't been my whole life. I really don't want you to think I've always been, you know, struggling with things or hard to work with. I've always prided myself on being pretty easygoing and a really reliable guy. 

It actually... it all just started about eight months ago. We were doing an ambulance transfer, and I ended up hurting my shoulder and my ribs. It wasn't anything I couldn't handle, I promise! I really didn't want to make a big fuss about it or complain to anyone. But... yeah, it was right after that happened when I started really needing to arrange things and make sure the order was just right. 

I hope it's okay that it started more recently like that, and not when I was young. Does that help you with your notes? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right timeline so I can be as helpful to you as possible.

When you finish arranging the equipment or repeating the numbers, is it mainly because you're trying to prevent a specific bad thing from happening—like harm to a patient or the station—or is it more that you just need to get rid of an uncomfortable feeling that something isn't 'right' yet?

Um... well, it's... I guess it's a little of both, maybe? But mostly... mostly I just want to make sure nothing bad happens. I really don't want to cause any trouble or have anyone get hurt. 

Like... the reason they actually sent me here to see you, um... it was because at the station, I kept moving the airway bags around. I was just putting them into a pattern that I... I just knew was right, you know? And I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud. 

My lieutenant, he... he told me to stop and step away, but I... I couldn't. I didn't want to be disrespectful to him, I swear! I'm usually really good about following orders. But it just felt like... like the whole bay would go bad, like something terrible would happen if I broke the sequence. I had to finish it to keep things safe. 

I really hope you don't think I'm a bad EMT for not listening to my lieutenant right then. I was just trying to protect everyone, I promise. Does... does that make sense? I hope I'm explaining it okay for you.

Um... I'm trying to think, but... no, I don't think I've ever noticed anything quite like that. I'm so sorry, doctor. I really hope I'm not making your job harder by not having a good answer for you there. 

I just... I haven't experienced that, I don't think. I really try to be super aware of how I'm doing, especially since people rely on me at work, but that one just doesn't sound familiar at all. 

Is... is it okay that I say no to that? I can keep thinking on it if you want me to, or we can come back to it. I just really want to make sure I'm giving you the right information and being as helpful as I can be.

I'm... I'm really sorry, doctor, but I didn't quite catch what you just asked. My mind just went a little blank for a second there. 

Could you please repeat the question for me? I just want to make sure I understand exactly what you're looking for so I can give you the best answer possible. I'd really hate to mess up your notes or give you the wrong idea. I hope it's not too much trouble to ask you to say it again! I just want to be as helpful as I can.

Besides physically arranging things or saying the numbers out loud, do you ever find yourself repeating certain words, numbers, or phrases silently in your head as a kind of mental ritual, even when you're not doing anything with your hands?

Um, silently in my head? Like, just thinking the numbers over and over? 

Um... I don't... I don't really think so. When I need to do the numbers, I usually have to actually say them out loud, like I was telling you before. I don't really just do it in my head. 

I mean, I think about work a lot, and I run through protocols in my head just to make sure I know them perfectly, because I really want to be the best EMT I can be. But it's not like a ritual or anything like that. It's just me trying to be prepared. 

I'm sorry if that's not the answer you were looking for. Is it... is it bad if I don't do that? I just want to make sure I'm giving you what you need. I hope I'm being helpful.

Outside of the moments when you're actually arranging things or saying the numbers, do you ever get sudden, unwanted worries pop into your mind—like a nagging fear that something bad will happen—even when you're not in the middle of doing the ritual?

Um, sudden worries... like a fear of something bad happening? 

I don't... no, I really don't think I get those. I mean, obviously, I care a whole lot about my job, so I always want to make sure I'm doing everything perfectly on a call. You know, just making sure everyone stays safe. But it's not like a... a sudden, nagging fear that just pops up out of nowhere when I'm at home or anything like that. 

I feel terrible, I feel like I just keep saying no to all your questions today. I'm so sorry if I'm not giving you the answers you need for your assessment. I promise I'm really trying to think hard about it, I just haven't noticed that happening to me. 

Am I... am I doing okay with all this? I really don't want to be a difficult patient or make your job harder. If you need me to explain anything else better, please just let me know. I really want to do this right for you.

Doctor, I'm so sorry, but I think you forgot to ask the question. I really want to answer it for you, but I didn't hear what you said. Did I miss it? I'm so sorry if I wasn't paying attention. Could you please ask me again? I promise I'm listening this time.

Oh, I'm so sorry, did you not ask a question? I just... I saw you looking at me and I thought maybe I missed something. I'm sorry, I don't mean to be awkward. I just want to make sure I'm following along properly. I'm ready whenever you are, doctor. I promise.

When you think about it now, do you recognize on some level that skipping the sequence wouldn't actually cause the ambulance bay or station to 'go bad,' or do you still feel, deep down, that it genuinely would cause real harm if you didn't complete it?

Um... that's a really good question, doctor. I... I want to be completely honest with you, even though it's a little embarrassing to admit. I don't want you to think I'm a bad EMT or anything, I really try so hard to be good at my job. But... deep down... yes, I really did feel like it would genuinely cause real harm. 

Actually, that's... that's kind of why they sent me here to see you. I was at the station, and I just kept moving the airway bags into this pattern—because I just knew it was the right pattern—and I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud. My lieutenant told me to stop, but I... I wouldn't step away when he told me to. I just couldn't, because it felt like the whole bay would go bad if I broke the sequence. 

I'm so sorry, I know that probably sounds really strange to hear. I hope I'm not making your assessment too complicated by saying that. Did I explain that okay for you? I really want to make sure I'm giving you what you need.

Um... doctor? I'm sorry, I hope I didn't say the wrong thing just now. You're... you're being a little quiet, and I just want to make sure I didn't mess up your assessment. 

Did... did you ask another question and I missed it again? Or did I give a bad answer before? I can try to explain it differently if you want, or we can talk about whatever else you need. I'm trying really hard to pay attention, I promise. I just want to be helpful and do this right for you.

I'm sorry, I'll just be quiet now so you can finish writing your notes. I know I'm probably talking way too much and I really don't want to interrupt your process or be a difficult patient. 

I just get a little nervous that I'm not giving you the right answers, or that I'm making your job harder. I'll just sit here and wait until you're ready. Just take your time, doctor. I'm ready whenever you have the next question for me. Is... is that okay?

doctor.intent: Establish the primary reason for today's visit
doctor.question: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Abnormal_Behavior
target_item.manifestation: They sent me here because at the station I kept moving the airway bags into a pattern I knew was right, repeating the dispatch numbers out loud, and I wouldn't step away when my lieutenant told me to stop because it felt like the whole bay would go bad if I broke the sequence.
target_item.reason: This is the first reply of the consultation, so I must return the chief complaint symptom code, which is S022.

patient.answer:
Um, hi Doctor. It's nice to meet you. I, uh... well, my lieutenant at the station actually sent me. It’s a little embarrassing, to be honest, and I really don't want to make a big deal out of it, but I want to be cooperative with you. 

I was just... I was organizing our equipment. The airway bags. I kept moving them into this specific pattern that I just knew was right, and I guess I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud while I did it. Just trying to be thorough, you know? But then my lieutenant told me to stop, and... I didn't step away. I didn't mean to be insubordinate or cause trouble, I swear, it's just... it felt like the whole ambulance bay would go bad if I broke the sequence right then. 

I hope I'm explaining that okay? I really am just trying to do the right thing, I promise. Does that make sense?

inference.note: Initial presentation shows compulsive ordering/counting behavior with magical thinking (breaking sequence will cause harm) and difficulty stopping despite instruction, suggesting OCD; rigidity/perfectionism raises OCPD; occupational stress (EMS work) raises possibility of anxiety/trauma-related checking behavior.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient recognizes the repeating/sequencing behavior as excessive or unreasonable (ego-dystonic, suggesting OCD) versus feeling it is simply the correct, sensible way to do things (ego-syntonic, suggesting a personality trait)
doctor.question: When you're doing that pattern with the equipment and repeating the numbers, do you feel like the urge is excessive or doesn't make sense, or does it feel like just the right and reasonable way to do the job?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient's insight into their repetitive behavior (whether they feel it's excessive/unreasonable or justified), which relates to ego-dystonic vs ego-syntonic traits often seen in OCD vs psychosis. This specific question about insight/reasonableness of the behavior is not covered in the symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Um... well, I guess when you put it like that, I can totally see how it might look a little excessive to someone else. I really don't want to be unreasonable, I promise. I know how it must have looked to my lieutenant. 

But in the moment, it just... it feels completely right. Like it's the only safe way to set up the bags. I just want to be thorough so nothing goes wrong on a call, you know?
